newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lufthansa manager bemoans German service levels.
newsitem.headline: Lufthansa manager bemoans German service levels.

text.p: A senior manager at German flag carrier Deutsche Lufthansa said on Thursday that Germany needed desperately to boost the quality of its service sector or miss out on the global boom in tourism.

Lufthansa board member Hemjoe Klein said such a move was particularly vital for the airline industry, where he estimated that some 80 percent of growth up until the year 2005 would come from tourist traffic.
"The question is: How do we improve the quality of our service sector in Germany?" Klein told a lunch organised by the American Chamber of Commerce in Berlin.
Klein said German service-providers were not yet focused strongly enough on the customer and that a complete change of mind-set was required.
"Being receptive to the customer is not a question of money or organisation...but of attitude," he added.
Klein said Germany's strong trade surplus hid an annual net deficit in the tourist industry of some 55 billion marks ($31.9 billion).

Germany's tourism industry, which benefits from attractions ranging from the Black Forest and the Bavarian Alps to the metropolitan pleasures of cities such as Berlin, Munich and Hamburg, employs some two million people and had revenues of 43 billion marks in 1995/96.
According to recently-published figures, the Germans themselves are the world's most avid international travellers. They spent an estimated 95 billion marks on overnight travel in 1995.

Klein said that airlines including Lufthansa needed not only continuously to monitor their own quality levels but had to rely on high standards being maintained by back-up infrastructure such as the airports they served.
Germany late last year took a major step in altering what many foreigners saw as one of the most irritating features of life in Germany by relaxing previously draconian shop opening laws.

Early indications suggested that service levels in the retail sector initially fell as many shops decided to stay open later without employing more staff, but since then the experiment has proved more of a success as more, albeit part-time, workers have been taken on.
